L238: The Volkswagen Beetle, officially the Volkswagen Type 1,^{【147†[a]】} is a 【126†small family car】 produced by the German company 【121†Volkswagen】 from 1938 to 2003.^{【148†[b]】} A global 【149†cultural icon】 known for its 【150†bug】-like design, the Beetle is widely regarded as 【151†one of the most influential cars of the 20th century】.
L239: Its production period of 65 years is the longest for any single generation of automobile.^{【152†[c]】} With 21.5 million units produced over twenty locations worldwide, the Beetle is the best-selling car of a single 【153†platform】 in history and the second best-selling car nameplate of the 20th century.
L240: The Beetle was conceived in the early 1930s, when the leader of 【154†Nazi Germany】, 【155†Adolf Hitler】, decided there was a need for a people's car—an inexpensive, simple, mass-produced car—to serve Germany's new road network, the 【156†Reichsautobahn】. Engineer 【124†Ferdinand Porsche】 and his design team began developing and designing the car in the early 1930s, but the fundamental design concept can be attributed to 【157†Béla Barényi】 in 1925, predating Porsche's^{【158†[d]】} claims by almost ten years.
L241: The result was the Volkswagen Type 1 and the introduction of the Volkswagen brand. Volkswagen initially slated production for the late 1930s, but the outbreak of 【159†World War II】 in 1939 delayed production until the war ended in 1945. The car was originally called the Volkswagen Type 1 and marketed simply as the Volkswagen; it was not until 1968 that it was officially named the "Beetle".
L242: Volkswagen implemented designations for the Beetle in the 1960s, including 1200, 1300, 1500, 1600, 1302, and 1303. The company introduced a series of large luxury models throughout the 1960s and 1970s—comprising the 【133†Type 3】, 【160†Type 4】 and 【161†K70】—to supplement the Beetle, but none of these models achieved the level of success that the Beetle did. In 1972, the Beetle surpassed the 【162†Ford Model T】 to become the 【163†best-selling car of all time】, a record it held for 25 years.
L243: Rapidly changing consumer preferences toward 【164†front-wheel drive】 compact hatchbacks in Europe prompted Volkswagen's gradual shift away from rear-wheel drive, starting with the 【165†Golf】 in 1974. In the late 1970s and 1980s, 【166†Japanese automakers】 began to dominate markets around the world, which contributed to the Beetle's declining popularity.
L244: The Beetle remains one of the best-selling cars of all time, and is the first to have over 20 million units produced. Over its lifespan, its design remained consistent, yet Volkswagen implemented over 78,000 updates. These modifications were mostly subtle, involving minor alterations to its exterior, interior, colours, and lighting. Some more noteworthy changes included the introduction of new engines, models and systems, such as improved technology or comfort.
L245: The Beetle maintains a substantial cultural influence, and is regarded as one of the most iconic vehicles in automotive history. Its success largely influenced the way automobiles are designed and marketed, and propelled Volkswagen's introduction of 【119†a Golf-based series of vehicles】.
L246: ## History
L247: 
L248: [【167†edit】]
L249: ### KdF-Wagen
L250: 
L251: [【168†edit】]
L252: In May 1934, during a meeting at Berlin's 【169†Kaiserhof Hotel】, the dictator of 【154†Nazi Germany】, 【155†Adolf Hitler】, insisted on the development of a vehicle that could accommodate two adults and three children while not using more than seven litres of fuel per 100 km (33.6 mpg US/40.4 mpg UK).^{【170†[5]】} All components were designed for a quick and inexpensive part exchange.
L253: As Hitler explained, the reason for choosing an 【171†air-cooled engine】 was the lack of a garage for every country doctor.^{【172†[6]】}^{【173†[7]】} On 22 June 1934, 【124†Ferdinand Porsche】 received a development contract from the 【174†Verband der Automobilindustrie】 (German Association of the Automotive Industry) for the prototype of an inexpensive and economical passenger car after Hitler decided there was a need for a people's car (in German, "volkswagen")—a car affordable and practical enough for lower-class people to own—to serve the country's new road network, the 【156†Reichsautobahn】.^{【175†[8]】}^{【176†[9]】} Although the Volkswagen car was primarily the conception of Porsche and Hitler, the idea of a "people's car" is much older than 【177†Nazism】, and has existed since the introduction of automotive mass production.^{【178†[10]】}
L254: Originally designated as the Type 60 by Porsche, the Beetle project involved a team of designers and engineers, comprising 【179†Erwin Komenda】, who specialised in the bodywork; Josef Kales, responsible for the engine design; 【180†Karl Rabe】, serving as the chief engineer; and Josef Mickl and Franz Xaver Reimspiess, the latter credited for devising the iconic Volkswagen badge.^{【181†[11]】} The project saw significant milestones in October 1935, with the completion of the first two Type-60 prototypes, identified as cars V1 (sedan) and V2 (convertible), denoted with a "V" (for Versuchs – "prototype"), signifying their status as a 【182†test car】.^{【183†[12]】} The testing of three additional V3 prototypes began on 11 July 1936, the first of which was driven to 【184†Obersalzberg】 and inspected by Hitler.
L255: Two V3s were delivered to Berlin in August for examination by other Nazi Party officials, who showed great interest in them.
L256: By June 1936, the V3s had undergone more than 50,000 km (31,000 mi) of testing across various types of terrain.^{【185†[13]】}^{【186†[14]】} A series of thirty W30 development models, commissioned by Porsche and manufactured by Daimler-Benz, underwent testing in early April 1937,^{【187†[15]】} covering a total distance of over 2,900,000 kilometres (1,800,000 mi).^{【188†[16]】} All vehicles featured the characteristic rounded design and included 【136†air-cooled】, rear-mounted 【189†engines】.^{【187†[15]】}^{【190†[17]】} A further batch of 44 VW38 pre-production cars produced in 1938 introduced split rear windows,^{【191†[18]】} and subsequently, Volkswagen introduced fifty VW39 cars, completed in July 1939.^{【192†[19]】}^{【193†[20]】}
L257: Two KdF cars on the 【156†Reichsautobahn】, c. (circa) 1943. Since the KdF was never delivered to the public,^{【194†[21]】} it is likely that this was an advertisement photo.
L258: 【195†Kraft durch Freude】 (Strength Through Joy, a political organisation aimed at providing the populace with leisure activities) was in charge of this project. 【196†Robert Ley】, the official heading Kraft durch Freude (KdF), announced in 1938 that every German would own a Volkswagen within ten years.^{【197†[22]】} However, there were challenges. Gasoline prices in Germany were high due to taxes, making it expensive for private car ownership.
L259: Gasoline was also primarily used for the military in the Nazi regime. Despite that, the regime saw the mass-produced car as a way to promote their system. It symbolised a shift from cars being a privilege for the wealthy to a dream that lower-class Germans could now fulfil. Hitler was particularly enthusiastic about it because the car could easily be adapted for military use.^{【198†[23]】}
L260: The KdF-Wagen was not 【199†series-produced】 before 【159†World War II】 because the 【200†Volkswagen plant】 at 【201†Fallersleben】 (now 【202†Wolfsburg】), founded in May 1938, was not yet completed.
L261: During the war, other German manufacturers were concurrently producing 【203†military vehicles】 and 【204†armaments】, so the series production of the Volkswagen car could not begin until peacetime; nevertheless, 210 KdF-Wagens were manufactured by the end of the war in May 1945.^{【205†[24]】}^{【206†[25]】} Following the cessation of hostilities, the 【207†British occupying forces】 brought the factory into operation.
L262: By the end of 1945, 1,785 Volkswagens had been built, delivered to the occupying powers and the 【208†postal service】.^{【209†[26]】}^{【210†[27]】}^{【206†[25]】}
L263: ### Design
L264: 
L265: [【211†edit】]
L266: The Beetle features a rear-located, air-cooled four-cylinder, 【212†boxer engine】 and rear-wheel drive in a two-door bodywork.
L267: It features a flat front windscreen, accommodating four passengers and providing luggage storage under the front bonnet and behind the rear seat, reaching a drag coefficient of 【213†Cd】=0.48.^{【214†[28]】}^{【215†[29]】} The bodywork attached with eighteen bolts to the Beetle's nearly flat 【216†platform chassis】 features a central structural tunnel.^{【217†[30]】} The front and rear suspension incorporate 【218†torsion bars】 and a front stabiliser bar, providing independent suspension at all wheels; however, the front axle was designed with double longitudinal trailing arms, whereas the rear axle was a 【219†swing axle】.^{【220†[31]】} 【221†Light alloy】 forms the Beetle's engine, transmission, and cylinder heads.^{【217†[30]】}
L268: ### Design controversies
L269: 
L270: [【222†edit】]
L271: 
L272: German-Bohemian engineer 【124†Ferdinand Porsche】 and his team were generally known as the original designers of the Volkswagen.^{【223†[32]】} However, there has been debate over whether he was the original designer. Rumours circulated suggesting that other designers, such as 【157†Béla Barényi】, 【224†Paul Jaray】, 【225†Josef Ganz】 and 【226†Hans Ledwinka】, may have influenced its design.
L273: 
L274: Béla Barényi
L275: In 1925, Austro-Hungarian automotive engineer Béla Barényi designed a car shaped similarly to the Beetle, more than five years before Porsche unveiled his initial "People's Car" design.^{【227†[33]】} Through a court ruling in 1953, Barényi successfully asserted his authorship and associated claims. He explained that he had previously elucidated the concept of the Beetle, which was already formulated in the 1920s, to Porsche in great detail.
L276: However, this concept was not protected sufficiently by 【228†patents】. Key elements of this concept included the air-cooled four-cylinder boxer engine at the rear, the transmission positioned in front of the rear axle, and the distinctive roundish shape.
L277: Dieter Landenberger, the head of Porsche's historical archive, later affirmed that Barényi played a "decisive role in the authorship of the later VW Beetle".^{【229†[34]】} Since then, Barényi has been known for conceiving the original car design.^{【230†[35]】}
L278: Paul Jaray
L279: Many assume that Paul Jaray shaped the car's body design through his aerodynamics calculations.^{【231†[36]】} According to a November 2021 update of research mentioned in the fifteenth report by the German newspaper 【232†Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung】, Jaray's findings influenced the design of "Hitler's streamlined KdF car", later known as the Beetle, which became the best-selling car globally after World War II.^{【233†[37]】} Jaray's research results in fluid mechanics for ground-bound vehicles extended beyond the Beetle, impacting the 【234†Tatra 77】 and other vehicles.
L280: His initial patents and publications date back to the early 1920s. Engineer Christian Binnebesel scientifically presented Jaray's significant contribution to streamline form in his 2008 dissertation.^{【235†[38]】}
L281: Josef Ganz
L282: Josef Ganz's potential early contributions to the original Beetle's development remained controversial for years and lacked clear clarification. Research suggests that his idea and the concept of a compact car played a significant role in the Beetle's development and its prototypes.^{【236†[39]】}^{【237†[40]】} Ganz personally drove a 【238†Hanomag Kommissbrot】 and a swing-axle Tatra, both of which featured elements such as a central tubular frame, independent wheel suspension, and a rear/mid-engine design.
L283: Ganz incorporated these technical features into his proposed vehicle designs. Hitler reportedly saw cars designed by Ganz at the 1933 【239†Berlin Auto Show】.^{【240†[41]】} The 【241†Standard Superior】, designed by Ganz for the Standard vehicle factory, featured an implied teardrop-shaped body on a central tubular frame with a rear swing axle, yet the engine was transversely installed in front of the axle, not longitudinally as a rear engine.^{【242†[42]】}^{【243†[43]】}
L284: Hans Ledwinka
L285: Austrian automobile designer 【226†Hans Ledwinka】, a contemporary of Porsche, worked for Czechoslovak company 【244†Tatra】.^{【245†[44]】} In 1931, Tatra built the 【246†V570】 prototype, which featured an 【247†air-cooled】 【248†flat-twin engine】 mounted at the rear.^{【249†[45]】} Hitler and Porsche both were influenced by the Tatras.^{【249†[45]】} Hitler, an avid automotive enthusiast, rode in Tatras multiple times during political tours of Czechoslovakia and had frequent dinners with Ledwinka.^{【249†[45]】} Following one such tour, Hitler remarked to Porsche, "This is the car for my roads."^{【249†[45]】}^{【250†[46]】} From 1933 onwards, Ledwinka and Porsche met regularly to discuss their designs, and Porsche admitted, "Well, sometimes I looked over his shoulder, and sometimes he looked over mine" while designing the Volkswagen.^{【249†[45]】} The 1936 【251†Tatra 97】 had a 1,749 cc, rear-located, rear-wheel drive, air-cooled four-cylinder 【212†boxer engine】.
L286: It accommodated five passengers in its compact four-door body, which provided luggage storage under the front bonnet and behind the rear seats.^{【243†[43]】}
L287: Just before the outbreak of 【159†World War II】, Tatra filed numerous legal claims against VW for patent infringement.^{【252†[47]】} Tatra launched a lawsuit that was halted only by 【253†Germany's invasion of Czechoslovakia】 in 1938, leading to the Nazi administration of the Tatra factory in October.
L288: Hitler instructed Tatra to focus exclusively on heavy trucks and diesel engines, discontinuing all car models except the V8-engined 【254†Tatra 87】.^{【243†[43]】} The issue resurfaced after World War II, and in 1965, Volkswagen paid Ringhoffer-Tatra one million 【255†Deutsche Marks】 in an out-of-court settlement.^{【256†[48]】}

L296: Sand-coloured VW Type 82E — a Wehrmacht Beetle on the 【259†Kübelwagen's】 underpinnings.
L297: The name Volkswagen was officially substituted by the term KdF (【260†Kraft durch Freude】, German for "Strength Through Joy") once Hitler ceremoniously laid the foundation stone for the Volkswagen factory on 26 May 1938.^{【261†[49]】}^{【262†[50]】} As part of this organisation, Volkswagen urged workers to "save five marks a week and get your car".^{【263†[51]】}^{【264†[52]】}^{【265†[53]】} Before the completion of the KdF factory, many Germans had already signed up for a savings plan to buy a car.
L298: At that time, Germany had fewer cars than other European countries. In 1930, there were only about 500,000 registered cars in Germany, while France and Great Britain had more than a million each, and the United States had more than 26 million.^{【266†[54]】}^{【267†[55]】} However, the onset of 【159†World War II】 hindered the distribution of the cars, and there was a lack of time for 【268†series production】.
L299: With the Volkswagen facility dedicated solely to wartime requirements, more than 330,000 KdF savers could not acquire their vehicles.^{【269†[56]】}^{【270†[57]】} Following the war, numerous KdF savers pressed for the receipt of a Volkswagen. When their request was denied, the VW saver initiative ensued, spanning several years.^{【271†[58]】}
L300: During the war, the factory predominantly built the 【259†Kübelwagen】 (Type 82),^{【272†[59]】}^{【273†[60]】} the 【274†Schwimmwagen】 (Type 166)^{【275†[61]】}^{【273†[60]】} and numerous other 【276†light utility vehicles】.
L301: These vehicles were derived mechanically from the Type 1 and used by the 【277†Wehrmacht】.^{【278†[62]】}^{【279†[63]】}^{【280†[64]】} These vehicles, including several hundred 【281†Kommandeurswagen】 (Type 87), featured a Type 1 Beetle body mounted on the robust chassis of the four-wheel-drive Type 86 Kübelwagen prototype.
L302: The Kommandeurswagen included a portal axle, a Schwimmwagen drivetrain, wider fenders, and oversized Kronprinz all-terrain tyres, reminiscent of the later 【282†Baja Bugs】.^{【283†[65]】} The production of the Kommandeurswagen persisted until 1944 when the production at the plant halted due to the extensive damage inflicted by the Allied air raids.^{【284†[66]】} Due to gasoline shortages late in the war, a few "Holzbrenner" (wood-burner) Beetles were built fueled with wood logs.^{【285†[67]】}
L303: The 【286†Porsche 64】 (pictured in 1981) was largely derived from the Beetle.
L304: 【260†Kraft durch Freude】 arranged an event for September 1939 to showcase Germany's 【287†Autobahn】 highway system and to promote the purported beginning of the production of the KdF-Wagen, involving a 1,500-kilometre (930 mi) journey from Berlin to Rome.^{【288†[68]】} Erwin Komenda supervised the development process, while Karl Froelich was responsible for creating official plans that they subsequently used to form a wooden scale model.
L305: The model was wind tunnel tested at 【289†Stuttgart University】 by Josef Mickl.^{【290†[69]】} Dubbed the "Berlin-Rome car", Porsche AG's engineers designed the Type 60 K 10, officially known as the 【286†Porsche 64】.^{【291†[70]】}^{【292†[71]】} Although the engineers produced three vehicles, they never made it to the race due to the 【293†outbreak of World War II】 before the scheduled date;^{【288†[68]】} two of them disappeared during the conflict.^{【294†[72]】} Austrian Otto Mathé acquired the third Berlin-Rome car and raced it throughout the 1950s, becoming the fastest in its class during the 1950 Alpine Cup.^{【295†[73]】} He continued to use it until his death in 1995.^{【296†[74]】}^{【297†[75]】}

L311: The Beetle was successful once it began production following the end of the war.^{【300†[76]】} On 11 April 1945, Stadt des KdF-Wagens bei Fallersleben, where 17,000 people lived, was officially designated 【202†Wolfsburg】.^{【301†[77]】}^{【302†[78]】} Official 【268†series manufacture】 of the 【128†saloon】 began on 27 December 1945;^{【303†[79]】} Volkswagen had produced 55 vehicles by the end of the year.^{【304†[80]】}^{【305†[81]】} The Volkswagen facility, initially slated for dismantling and transportation to Britain under American control in 1945, faced a lack of interest from British car manufacturers; an official report stated that "The vehicle does not meet the fundamental technical requirement of a motor-car [...] it is quite unattractive to the average buyer [...] To build the car commercially would be a completely uneconomic enterprise." Nonetheless, the factory remained operational by producing cars for the 【306†British Army】.^{【307†[82]】} Allied dismantling policy changed from late 1946 to mid-1947.
